entry.title: Counting days is not measuring phase

link.title: Counting days is not measuring phase

entry.content:
Most datasets and studies that work with the menstrual cycle assign phase by counting days from the last period. The count is a proxy for an underlying hormonal state, and a weak one. In 1,498 cycles from 157 women tracked with a urinary-hormone monitor, a fixed calendar rule placed a session in its intended cycle phase 53 to 60 percent of the time, depending on the window. The physiology these labels stand in for varies across the cycle, so a label that is wrong a third to a half of the time is not a small measurement detail. It sets a ceiling on what any downstream analysis or model can recover.

Why the phase label matters

Women are half the population, yet the datasets behind health AI and motion science were built almost entirely on male or sex-neutral physiology (Jiang et al., The Lancet Digital Health). Where the cycle is considered at all, it enters as an estimated independent variable: a session is labelled follicular or luteal, and outcomes are compared across those labels.

Hormonal state across the cycle is associated with measurable shifts in neuromuscular function, strength, sleep and cognition. A meta-analysis of 22 studies reported moderate shifts in maximal muscle strength favouring the late follicular phase (Niering et al., 2024), and grip and isokinetic torque vary across biochemically confirmed phases in physically active women (Weidauer et al., 2020).

The difficulty is that the label is usually estimated, not measured. Calendar counting and basal body temperature stand in for hormonal confirmation, and each introduces error at the exact point where the signal is read. Models trained on data labelled this way inherit the error, and biomedical AI systems already underperform for women when trained on non-representative data (Cirillo et al., 2020; Joshi, 2024). Before asking whether a cycle effect exists, it is worth asking how often the label naming the phase is correct.

The data

The Marquette Menstrual Cycle Data contains day-by-day records from women using an electronic fertility monitor that reads urinary luteinising hormone and an estrogen metabolite (Fehring, 2012; Fehring et al., 2013). The monitor marks a hormonally defined peak day near ovulation, which gives a per-cycle anchor that calendar counting does not.

I used the monitor-tracked cycles, 1,498 cycles from 157 women, and took the peak day as the ovulation reference. The question is deliberately simple: without the monitor, assigning phase by counting days instead, how often would you be right?

Ovulation does not happen on day 14

Ovulation fell on a median of day 15, with an interquartile range of day 14 to 18. It landed exactly on day 14, the textbook value, in 15 percent of cycles. Luteal length was also variable, with a median of 13 days and an interquartile range of 12 to 14.

A woman’s own history helps, but only partly. The within-woman standard deviation of the ovulation day was 2.2 days, and the intraclass correlation was 0.64. About a third of the variance in ovulation timing sits within women across their own cycles, so a personalised estimate built from a woman’s average still leaves a two-day spread around any single cycle. The day-14 assumption is wrong for most cycles, and a woman’s own mean does not pin down the current one.

A day-21 visit is not the luteal phase

Scheduling makes the cost concrete. The table below shows how often three common rules place a session in its intended window, across the same 1,498 cycles.

Target window Fixed calendar day Backward from usual length Backward from actual length
Mid-luteal (ovulation +5 to +9) 60% 66% 77%
Periovulatory (ovulation -2 to +1) 53% 57% 73%

Two things follow. A fixed-day visit misses its intended phase in a quarter to nearly half of cases, and the direction of counting matters. Counting backward from the realised length of the cycle, when it is known, is consistently better than counting forward from the last period, because luteal length is more stable than follicular length.

The statistical cost

Phase misclassification does not only mislabel cases, it attenuates the effect under study. When a fraction of sessions carry the wrong phase, a real difference between phases is diluted toward zero, and more participants are needed to recover the same power. Under a simplified all-or-none misclassification model, the inflation in required sample size ranged from about 1.7 for actual-length backward counting to 2.8 for the fixed day-21 rule. These figures are a rough bound rather than a precise correction.

The direction, though, is not in doubt. A single session per woman, scheduled by calendar, detects only large effects, and part of the inconsistency in the cycle literature is likely noise in the phase label rather than the absence of an effect. Within-woman designs, with sessions timed by a hormonal marker such as a urinary LH test, remove most of this penalty.

What this shows, and what to do

Although the monitor gives a hormonally defined peak day, it is a urinary marker rather than serum, so it bounds how well calendar counting could do rather than defining ground truth exactly. The cohort is also women with regular cycles tracking to conceive, so the spread in the wider population, including adolescence and the perimenopausal transition, is likely wider, not narrower. The analysis is exploratory and the sample-size figures are illustrative.

The practical implications are specific:

  • Confirm phase with a hormonal marker wherever the design allows it.
  • Where it does not, count backward from the realised cycle length rather than forward from the last period, and do not treat day 14 and day 21 as fixed.
  • Report the phase-assignment method explicitly. An effect measured against confirmed phase and one measured against a calendar label are not the same measurement.

For anyone building cycle-aware wearables or models, the label is the foundation. If it is wrong a third of the time, everything trained on it inherits that error. Counting days is cheap. It is also wrong often enough to matter.

Data, code and references

The analysis and notebooks are in the public repository Hormones-Brain-Motion. The source is the Marquette Menstrual Cycle Data.

  2. Niering M, et al. Sports. 2024.
  3. Weidauer LA, et al. Journal of Musculoskeletal and Neuronal Interactions. 2020.
  4. Cirillo D, et al. npj Digital Medicine. 2020.
  5. Joshi A. Frontiers in Big Data. 2024.
  6. Fehring RJ. Menstrual Cycle Data. Marquette University e-Publications, 2012. https://epublications.marquette.edu/data_nfp/7
  7. Fehring RJ, Schneider M, Raviele K, et al. Contraception. 2013. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.contraception.2012.10.010

entry.title: What resting EEG can and cannot say about the menstrual cycle

link.title: What resting EEG can and cannot say about the menstrual cycle

entry.content:
A public EEG dataset lets you ask a direct question: do resting brain rhythms differ between women on hormonal contraception and naturally cycling women, or across the menstrual cycle? With 37 contraceptive users and 32 non-users, the answer this dataset can support is that it cannot tell. After correction for multiple comparisons, no spectral measure differed between groups. That is not evidence that the cycle leaves resting EEG unchanged. It is a dataset too small to detect anything but a large effect, labelled by a method too coarse to place the phase.

The dataset and the test

ds007615 (Normannseth et al., 2025) contains resting-state EEG from 69 women, 37 using hormonal contraception and 32 naturally cycling. I compared seven standard spectral measures between the two groups, including absolute and relative alpha power and the individual alpha peak frequency, and corrected for the seven tests with the Holm procedure.

Nothing survives correction

No measure differed between groups after correction. The largest raw effect was absolute alpha power, with a standardised difference of d = 0.48, but its 95% confidence interval ran from −0.00 to 0.96: consistent with a moderate effect and equally consistent with none. Relative alpha power (d = 0.33) and individual alpha peak frequency (d = −0.36) were smaller and also non-significant.

What the sample could have detected

The useful question is not whether the test was significant, but what it could have found. The minimum detectable effect for the contraceptive contrast was 0.69 SD. For a luteal-versus-other comparison within the naturally cycling women, it was 1.13 SD. Effects smaller than that were never in reach. Detecting a moderate between-groups effect (d = 0.5) at conventional power would need roughly 64 women per group, about twice this dataset.

A within-woman design changes the arithmetic. Measuring the same women at two cycle points, rather than comparing different women once, would bring the minimum detectable effect down to about 0.35 SD with 27 women, assuming a within-subject correlation of 0.8. The gain comes from removing between-person variation, which in resting EEG is large.

The phase labels are coarse too

Power is only half the problem. The phase labels in a dataset like this are assigned by counting days, not by measuring hormones. Here the cycle is divided into fixed day ranges (1–6, 7–12, 14+), and a binary follicular/luteal split places the ovulatory window into the luteal class. Recomputing the label by counting backward from each woman’s cycle length changes it for 14 of 26 cycles. A comparison built on these labels is comparing noisy groups, which widens the confidence intervals further. It is the same calendar problem that undermines day-based phase assignment elsewhere, now sitting on top of an already underpowered test.

What would answer the question

The honest reading of ds007615 is that it does not answer the question, and it says why: too few women, measured once, labelled by calendar. A dataset that could answer it would measure the same women across the cycle, with phase confirmed by a hormonal marker rather than a date. That is a different design, not a larger version of this one.

Data, code and references

The analysis and notebooks are in the public repository Hormones-Brain-Motion.

  1. Pritschet L, et al. NeuroImage. 2020.
  2. Normannseth, et al. Frontiers in Human Neuroscience. 2025.
  3. OpenNeuro dataset ds007615. https://doi.org/10.18112/openneuro.ds007615.v1.0.0
entry.summary: A public EEG dataset of 69 women cannot separate a cycle or contraceptive effect from noise. A power and labeling analysis.

entry.title: Does a wrist-activity model underperform for women?

link.title: Does a wrist-activity model underperform for women?

entry.content:
A common argument for building female-specific health data is that models trained mostly on men underperform for women. It is worth testing directly rather than assuming. Using two public datasets, a wrist-activity recognition benchmark and a national accelerometer survey, I looked for a sex or hormonal-status effect on what the model learns and on the measured activity itself. At the resolution these datasets work in, the effect is small enough to miss. That does not retire the argument. It locates where it applies.

A wrist-activity model barely registers sex

CAPTURE-24 (Chan et al., 2024) pairs wrist accelerometer data with camera-confirmed activity labels for 151 adults, 99 women and 52 men. I trained a gradient-boosted classifier on 32 standard features to predict four coarse activity classes, and matched the training sets on age across 50 resamples so that sex, not age, drove any difference.

Macro F1 sat at 0.67 to 0.68 everywhere. Training a model on a woman’s own sex rather than on a mixed set raised her macro F1 by 0.004 (95% CI −0.003 to 0.011). For men the gain was essentially zero. Between-person variation dwarfed both, with a standard deviation of 0.088 across individuals. Of ten per-class comparisons, exactly one had a confidence interval excluding zero: light activity was classified better for women, by 0.015 F1. For coarse wrist activity recognition, a model trained without regard to sex does not measurably underperform for women.

The population signal points the same way

The national data agree. In NHANES 2013–14 (3,815 adults with valid wrist accelerometry), women averaged 0.80 thousand MIMS per day more activity than men after age adjustment, so sex does move the aggregate. Hormonal status within women did not. Comparing menopausal and still-menstruating women aged 40 to 59, the activity difference was d = −0.07 (95% CI −0.46 to 0.32), indistinguishable from zero. Across 679 menstruating women whose measured estradiol spanned a 25-fold range, there was no association between estradiol and daily activity (d = 0.03 per doubling, CI −0.03 to 0.09). NHANES carries no cycle-day information, so this speaks to hormonal status and level, not to within-cycle timing.

Where the gap actually is

These are null results, and they are worth stating plainly rather than explaining away. At the resolution of four activity classes and daily activity volume, neither sex nor hormonal status changes the model or the measure enough to matter. The claim that models underperform for women is not wrong in general. It needs to be made where it bites: fine-grained tasks, specific physiological signals, and outcomes known to track hormones, rather than coarse activity summaries.

The same logic applies to collecting new data. A dataset that can show a cycle effect has to resolve the cycle, with confirmed phase and repeated measures, which is exactly what population accelerometry and day-labelled benchmarks lack.

The narrow conclusion

Coarse wrist activity is close to sex-neutral and hormone-neutral in these datasets. It is the wrong place to look for the gender data gap, and a weak place to argue it from. The gap is real where the resolution is fine enough to see it.

Data, code and references

The analysis and notebooks are in the public repository Hormones-Brain-Motion.

  1. Cirillo D, et al. npj Digital Medicine. 2020.
  2. Joshi A. Frontiers in Big Data. 2024.
  3. Chan et al. Scientific Data. 2024. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-024-03960-3
  4. NHANES 2013–2014, National Center for Health Statistics. https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/
entry.summary: Testing the gender data gap on two public datasets. At coarse activity resolution, sex and hormonal status barely move the model or the measure.
